To display and store more random effects, you can increase matsize. Otherwise, you can use the showreffects() and show() options on replay or use bayesstats summary after estimation to display subsets of the remaining random effects.

name: j_bayes_grubin_conv
title: Convergence rules for the Gelman-Rubin statistic

sections.Convergence rules for the Gelman-Rubin s: The Gelman-Rubin (1992) statistic convergence statistic, Rc, is a diagnostic used for assessing the convergence of MCMC based on multiple chains. Rc measures the between-chains variability relative to the within-chain variability. If all chains have converged, Rc should be close to 1. Brooks and Gelman (1998) suggest that the MCMC convergence can be declared when Rc is less than 1.2 for all model parameters. A more stringent convergence rule, Rc < 1.1, is often used in practice. See Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic in [BAYES] bayesstats grubin for details. When you simulate multiple chains using bayesmh or bayes or subsequently use bayesstats grubin to check MCMC convergence, the commands report the maximum value of Rc across all model parameters (except random-effects parameters for multilevel models) in the header. In this way, you can quickly assess whether some of the above convergence rules are satisfied for all parameters. With bayesstats grubin, you can use option sort to list model parameters in descending order of their convergence statistics Rc. The parameters with the largest values of Rc will be listed first, making it easier to verify their convergence. For multilevel models, convergence statistics are not reported for the random-effects parameters by default. If these parameters are of primary interest in your study, you should use option showreffects or showreffects(reref) to obtain convergence statistics for all random-effects parameters or for their subset reref. Also see Convergence diagnostics using multiple chains in [BAYES] bayesmh, Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic in [BAYES] bayesstats grubin, and Convergence of MCMC in [BAYES] bayesmh.
sections.References: Brooks, S. P., and A. Gelman. 1998. General methods for monitoring convergence of iterative simulations. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 7: 434-455. Gelman, A., and D. B. Rubin. 1992. Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science 7: 457-472.

sections.What is maximum Gelman-Rubin Rc?: When you simulate multiple chains using bayesmh or bayes, the commands report the maximum value of the Gelman-Rubin convergence statistic, Rc, across all model parameters (except random-effects parameters for multilevel models) in the header. This statistic is used for assessing the convergence of multiple Markov chains. By looking at the maximum value, you can quickly assess whether convergence rules are satisfied for all parameters. When the maximum Rc is larger than 1.2, you should suspect nonconvergence and investigate your model further; see Convergence rules for the Gelman-Rubin statistic and bayesstats grubin for details.

sections.Gelman-Rubin Ru: The Gelman-Rubin Ru statistic is an upper confidence limit for the Rc diagnostic statistic used for assessing the convergence of Markov chains. Ru is calculated with respect to a prespecified coverage probability, 0.95 by default, and assumes that the posterior distribution is normal. In a perfect case of convergence, Rc estimates are less than the corresponding Ru estimates for all model parameters. Often, this is a too strict condition, and we consider the convergence test to have passed when the maximum Rc is less than 1.1. For the detailed Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic, use the bayesstats grubin command.

sections.Random initial state not feasible: When you specify option initrandom with bayes or bayesmh and use diffuse priors, the command may not always find a good initial state. In that case, it will produce error message "could not find feasible random initial state". For example, if you are using bayes with default priors, option initrandom will generate initial values for regression coefficients from the normal distribution with zero mean and a variance of 10,000 and will likely produce large values for the coefficients. For some likelihood models, large coefficients may produce zero values of the likelihood and thus missing values for the log likelihood. In such cases, we recommend using default initial values, specifying more informative priors, or providing your own initial values.

name: j_bayes_nchainsinit
title: Default initial values with multiple chains

sections.Default initial values with multiple cha: Option nchains() with bayesmh or the bayes prefix generates multiple simulation chains. Each chain should use different initial values for model parameters. By default, maximum likelihood estimates (if available) are used as initial values for the first chain, and random initial values are used for subsequent chains. Whenever feasible, random initial values are generated from the prior distributions; see How are default initial values generated? for details. Default initial values are provided for convenience. To detect nonconvergence, you should use overdispersed initial values with multiple chains. Randomly generated default initial values are not guaranteed to produce overdispersed initial values for all chains. To fully explore convergence, we recommend that you specify your own initial values with multiple chains; see How do I specify initial values for multiple chains? To see the initial values used, you can specify option initsummary during estimation. You can also check initial values prior to estimation by specifying option dryrun. The initial values are also stored in matrix e(init) after estimation. See Specifying initial values in [BAYES] bayesmh and Initial values in [BAYES] bayes.
sections.How are default initial values generated: Option nchains() with bayesmh or bayes, by default, generates random initial values for model parameters for all but the first chain. Random initial values are generated from the prior distributions whenever feasible, but you can always specify your own. For improper priors flat, jeffreys, and jeffreys(#), bayesmh and the bayes prefix cannot draw random initial values directly from these priors. Doing so would typically produce extreme values for model parameters for which the log likelihood would be missing. See Specifying initial values in [BAYES] bayesmh and Initial values in [BAYES] bayes for details about how bayesmh and the bayes prefix generate default initial values with multiple chains. We recommend that, particularly with these priors, you provide your own initial values for multiple chains; see How do I specify initial values for multiple chains?
sections.How do I specify initial values for mult: In the presence of multiple chains, you may often need to specify your own initial values. bayesmh and bayes provide options for you to do this: init1() specifies initial values for the first chain, init2() for the second chain, and so on. The specification of options init#() is the same as that of option initial(), which specifies initial values when there is only one chain; see bayesmh, initial() and bayes, initial() for details. In the presence of multiple chains, option initial() is synonymous with option init1() and specifies initial values for the first chain. Suppose you have three chains. You can specify initial values for all three chains using options init#(): . ..., init1({a} 0 {b} 0) init2({a} 100 {b} 0.5) init3({a} -10 {b} 1) Or you can specify initial values only for the second chain and use the default initial values for chains 1 and 3: . ..., init2({a} 100 {b} .5) Or you can specify initial values for any combination of chains. In the above, we used fixed initial values. We can also generate initial values randomly. For example, we generate random initial values from a normal distribution for parameter {a} and from a uniform distribution for parameter {b} by typing . ..., init1({a} rnormal(0,1) {b} runiform(0,0.1)) > init2({a} rnormal(100,1) {b} runiform(0.4,0.6)) > init3({a} rnormal(-10,1) {b} runiform(0.9,1)) We can use other random-number functions. More generally, we can use any Stata expression that evaluates to a number to specify initial values. For convenience, there is also option initall(), which applies the same specification for initial values to all chains. This option can be useful when random initial values are used for all chains. For example, . ..., initall({a} rnormal(0, 100) {b} runiform(0,1)) Although different initial values will be used for all chains, they are not guaranteed to be overdispersed. To ensure that initial values are overdispersed, you will need to provide your own initial values for all chains. You should not specify fixed initial values in initall() because the same initial values will be used by all chains. See Specifying initial values in [BAYES] bayesmh, Initial values in [BAYES] bayes, and Multiple chains using overdispersed initial values in [BAYES] bayesmh.
sections.Could not find feasible initial values w: You specified option nchains() with bayesmh or bayes to simulate multiple chains but received a warning message "could not find feasible initial state" for some of the chains. If you specified your own initial values for the chains that failed, check the feasibility of these initial values. Otherwise, you are likely having trouble with the default random initialization of the parameters. Random initial values are generated when you specify option nchains() or option initrandom and when you use random-number functions to specify your own initial values. When random initial values are generated from prior distributions, extreme values may be produced for model parameters for some prior distributions, especially for noninformative priors. This may lead to missing log-likelihood values. The commands will attempt to generate several different sets of initial values before terminating the simulation of a particular chain and issuing the warning message. In this case, you must specify your own initial values for that chain; see How do I specify initial values for multiple chains? See Specifying initial values in [BAYES] bayesmh and Initial values in [BAYES] bayes.

name: j_bayes_remargl
title: Why is log marginal-likelihood not reported for multilevel models?

sections.Why is log marginal-likelihood not repor: The bayes prefix does not report the log marginal-likelihood (LML) by default for multilevel models. Bayesian multilevel models contain many parameters because, in addition to regression coefficients and variance components, they also estimate individual random effects. The computation of the LML involves the inverse of the determinant of the sample covariance matrix of all parameters, and loses its accuracy as the number of parameters grows. For high-dimensional models such as multilevel models, the computation of the LML can be time consuming, and its accuracy may become unacceptably low. Because it is difficult to access the levels of accuracy of the computation for all multilevel models, the LML is not reported by default. For multilevel models containing a small number of random effects, you can use the remargl option to compute and display the LML. When you specify the remargl option, the LML may still not be available for some models; see Why is log marginal-likelihood reported missing? for details.

name: j_bayes_toomanyre
title: Too many MCMC estimates to save when fitting Bayesian multilevel models

sections.Too many MCMC estimates to save when fit: You are trying to fit a Bayesian multilevel model containing many random effects. Unlike frequentist models, Bayesian models do not integrate out the individual random effects but estimate them together with other model parameters. Thus MCMC estimates are saved for all individual random effects in addition to other model parameters. To accommodate this, you must increase the limit for the maximum number of variables in your dataset (see set maxvar) to the total number of parameters in your model, including random effects plus one. The total number of parameters for which MCMC estimates can be saved in a simulation file cannot exceed the limit for the maximum number of variables minus one. This limit is specific to each edition of Stata and is the largest in Stata/MP. If you are interested only in the estimates of model parameters, but not the random effects themselves, you may consider specifying the exclude() option with bayesmh or bayes to prevent saving MCMC estimates of random effects. If you specify the exclude() option, the log marginal-likelihood and some postestimation features such as the computation of Bayes factors will not be available. However, their accuracy with high-dimensional models can be questionable, so this may not be a big loss. You may decide to exclude all random effects or only a subset of them. Keeping several random effects in the MCMC sample may be useful for checking convergence and for other model diagnostics.

sections.Adaptation continues during simulation: At the bottom of the parameter-estimates table, you may see a note about adaptation continuing during simulation. Adaptation is part of Metropolis-Hastings sampling and thus does not apply to the blocks of parameters updated using Gibbs sampling. You will typically see this message when you increase the number of adaptive iterations by using option adaptation(maxiter()) without correspondingly increasing the length of the burn-in period with option burnin(). This note does not necessarily indicate a problem. It simply notifies you that the proposal distribution is still in the period of adaptation after the burn-in period. This is often the case with so-called continuous adaptation such as diminishing adaptation, when parameters are allowed to adapt continuously during the burn-in and simulation periods, but they adapt less and less as the algorithm proceeds. By default, bayesmh does not perform diminishing adaptation and thus notifies you when adaptation continues during simulation. The default adaptation settings of bayesmh are chosen such that the adaptation stops after the burn-in period, regardless of whether the adaptation tolerance is met. (See Adaptation tolerance is not met for more information.) You can request diminishing adaptation by specifying a value other than the default of 0 in option adaptation(gamma()).

sections.Adaptation tolerance is not met: At the bottom of the parameter-estimates table, you may see a note about the adaptation tolerance not being met in at least one of the blocks of parameters. Adaptation is part of Metropolis-Hastings sampling and thus does not apply to the blocks of parameters updated using Gibbs sampling. This note does not necessarily indicate a problem. It simply notifies you that the default target acceptance rate as specified in option adaptation(tarate()) has not been reached within the tolerance specified in option adaptation(tolerance()). The default used for the target acceptance rate corresponds to the theoretical asymptotically optimal acceptance rate of 0.44 for a block with one parameter and 0.234 for a block with multiple parameters. The rate is derived for a specific class of models and does not necessarily represent the optimal rate for all models. If your MCMC converged, you can safely ignore this note. Otherwise, you need to investigate your model further. One remedy is to increase the burn-in period, which automatically increases the adaptation period, or more specifically, the number of adaptive iterations as controlled by option adaptation(maxiter()).

sections.Predictions with Bayesian evaluators: When you use an evaluator with bayesmh, you can use bayespredict to compute Bayesian predictions only if your evaluator implements sampling from the outcome distribution, that is, the data distribution (likelihood) conditional on the model parameters. Within your evaluator, you should check the value of the global macro MH_predict. If it is 1, you should generate the samples from the outcome distributions and store them in the corresponding temporary variables provided by the global macros MH_predict_y#. You should also compute and store the expected values for the outcomes in the corresponding temporary variables provided by the global macros MH_predict_mu#. If the value of MH_predict is not 1, you should perform your log-likelihood or log-posterior computations as described in User-defined evaluators of [BAYES] bayesmh evaluators. If your evaluator implements predictions, you should also specify suboption predict in bayesmh's option evaluator() or llevaluator() to let bayespredict know that predictions are supported. Otherwise, bayespredict will issue an error message that predictions are not supported. See Evaluators with predictions in [BAYES] bayespredict and Evaluators with predictions in [BAYES] bayesmh evaluators.

sections.High autocorrelation after 500 lags: You fit a Bayesian model using bayesmh or bayes and receive a note at the bottom of the output table that there is a high autocorrelation after 500 lags. What does this mean and is it a problem? High autocorrelation after 500 lags means that the correlation between the MCMC estimates that are 500 iterations apart is still above 0.01, the value determined by option corrtol(). The presence of autocorrelation in the MCMC sample is a known property of any MCMC sampling algorithm, but for well-behaved models and efficient sampling algorithms the autocorrelation should decrease as the lag increases. In other words, the MCMC estimates should become less correlated the further apart they are. When the autocorrelation remains high and does not become negligible as the lag increases, for example, after 500 lags, you should investigate your model carefully. High autocorrelation of the MCMC estimates is an indication of low efficiency or slow mixing in the MCMC sample. It may be due to nonconvergence or due to the presence of highly correlated parameters in the model. The lack of convergence is a problem that you will need to address. You can visually check for convergence, for example, by using bayesgraph diagnostics; also see Convergence of MCMC in BAYES bayesmh for details. Once convergence is established, the presence of high autocorrelation will typically mean low precision for some parameter estimates in the model. Depending on the magnitudes of the parameters and your research objective, you may be satisfied with the obtained precision, in which case you can ignore the reported note. If the level of precision is unacceptable, you may try to reduce autocorrelation in your model. We recommend you try to do it even if the level of precision is acceptable to you. To reduce autocorrelation, you must first identify the parameters with high autocorrelation. These parameters will also have low efficiencies and thus low effective sample sizes (ESS). You can use bayesstats ess to obtain efficiencies and ESS for all model parameters. For parameters with the lowest values, you can use bayesgraph matrix to check for correlation between them. Once you identify the parameters with high autocorrelation, consider how they are specified in the model. Are all of your model parameters identifiable given the used prior distributions? For instance, if you are using noninformative priors, can all of your parameters be estimated reliably using only the data? If not, you should either simplify the model or consider specifying more informative priors. Can you reparameterize your model to improve the mixing of the MCMC sampler? For example, in a two-level model, a constant term can be viewed as its own parameter with random-effects prior distribution centered around zero or as a hyperparameter with random-effects prior distribution centered around the constant term; see Two-level random-intercept model or panel-data model in BAYES bayesmh. Blocking of parameters (Improving efficiency of the MH algorithm -- blocking of parameters in BAYES bayesmh) and using other more efficient samplers (Gibbs and hybrid MH sampling in BAYES bayesmh) can help lower autocorrelation. Finally, you may consider subsampling or thinning the chain by using option thinning() to reduce autocorrelation, but this will often substantially increase simulation time. If you are fitting a multilevel model using noninformative priors, you are likely to encounter high autocorrelation for some parameter estimates. Unlike frequentist models, Bayesian models do not integrate out the individual random effects, but estimate them together with other model parameters. This substantially increases the dimensionality of the model and often makes it difficult to estimate all parameters with high precision. For instance, the estimates of variance components often have low precision. Also, fixed-effects parameters are often correlated with the corresponding random-effects parameters such as the constant term and random intercepts. As we mentioned earlier, the presence of high autocorrelation does not necessarily mean that all of your results are unreliable. If high autocorrelation pertains to some of the estimates of individual random effects, but you are mainly interested in regression coefficients and they have low autocorrelation and thus high precision, the existence of high autocorrelation among the random-effects estimates may not be that relevant to you. To summarize, the presence of high autocorrelation in your MCMC sample may or may not be a concern. Provided the model converged, the impact of high autocorrelation on the precision of parameter estimates will depend on the data, the model, and your research objective. We do recommend that you try to follow the steps described above to reduce the autocorrelation. See Specifying MCMC sampling procedure in BAYES bayesmh for more information.

name: j_bayesmh_marglmiss
title: Why is log marginal-likelihood reported missing?

sections.Why is log marginal-likelihood reported: The log marginal-likelihood (LML) could not be computed. This will often be the case when the size of the MCMC sample is very small. The computation of the LML involves the inverse of the determinant of the sample covariance matrix of the parameters. When the MCMC sample size is small, which often leads to having very few distinct simulated parameter values in the sample, the determinant of the matrix evaluates to 0, and the LML value becomes missing. The remedy is to specify a larger MCMC sample size in option mcmcsize(). Also, estimation of the LML becomes unstable for high-dimensional models such as multilevel models and may result in a missing value. A missing value is also reported when you specify the exclude() option with bayesmh and when you use the Laplace-Metropolis approximation, because this approximation requires simulation results for all parameters. When an LML is missing, Bayes factors computed by bayesstats ic and posterior model probabilities computed by bayestest model will also be missing. You can try using the marglmethod(hmean) option with these commands to use the harmonic-mean approximation of the LML, although this approximation is typically less precise.

name: j_bayesmh_nchains_avg
title: What are average log marginal-likelihood, acceptance rate, and efficiencies?

sections.What are average log marginal-likelihood: You specified option nchains() with bayesmh or the bayes prefix, and the header now reports Avg log marginal-likelihood, Avg acceptance rate, and Avg efficiencies. With multiple chains, the commands report an average value computed across chains for the log marginal-likelihood, acceptance rate, and efficiency. For models with multiple parameters, average values of minimum, maximum, and average efficiencies are reported. You can use option chainsdetail to see these values separately for each chain.

sections.Default priors in bmaregress: For convenience, the bmaregress command provides default priors for models and parameter g of a Zellner's g prior for regression coefficients. It uses the default beta-binomial prior with shape parameters of one on the model space, which assumes the uniform prior for the model size, and the default benchmark (fixed) prior for the g parameter. You can change them by specifying the mprior() and gprior() options, respectively. Default priors are provided for convenience. They are chosen based on the recommendations in the literature, which found them to be fairly uninformative in a variety of cases. But they may not apply to all cases. You should carefully evaluate the choice of priors and specify the priors that are appropriate for your model and research questions. You cannot simply rely on the provided defaults. You should also consider various priors to check the sensitivity of the results to the prior assumptions. See Priors in Introduction to BMA for linear regression in [BMA] bmaregress.

name: j_bma_jointness_threshold
title: Jointness as a measure of variable-inclusion dependence

sections.Jointness as a measure of variable-inclu: Jointness assesses the tendency of two covariates to be included together or exclusively across the model space. Below, we provide the thresholds for the Doppelhofer{ch_endash}Weeks and Ley{ch_endash}Steel measures. Thresholds for the Doppelhofer{ch_endash}Weeks measure DW Interpretation (-infinity, -2) Strong disjointness [-2, -1) Significant disjointness [-1, 1] Independent inclusion (1, 2] Significant jointness (2, infinity) Strong jointness Thresholds for Ley{ch_endash}Steel measures LS2LS1*Interpretation [0, 0.01)[0, 0.01)Decisive disjointness [0.01, 0.03)[0.01, 0.03)Very strong disjointness [0.03, 0.1)[0.03, 0.09)Strong disjointness [0.1, 0.22)[0.09, 0.18)Favorable disjointness [0.22, 3)[0.18, 0.75)Independent inclusion [3, 10)[0.75, 0.91)Favorable jointness [10, 30)[0.91, 0.97)Strong jointness [30, 100)[0.97, 0.99)Very strong jointness [100, infinity)[0.99, 1]Decisive jointness * rounded to 0.01 based on LS1 = LS2/(1 + LS2) Thresholds for Yule's Q and modified Yule's Q measures The values of Q above 0.7 suggest very strong jointness, and the values less than -0.7 suggest very strong disjointness. The values close to 0 (-0.3 < Q < 0.3) suggest independent inclusion.

name: j_bmaregress_coefs
title: How do I interpret BMA coefficients in bmaregress?

sections.How do I interpret BMA coefficients in b: bmaregress reports model-averaged estimates for the coefficients. The averaging is appropriate for parameters that have the same interpretation in all visited models, such as the intercept (after centering) and the error variance. But the interpretation of (partial) regression coefficients depends on the predictors included in the model and may change when the included predictors change. This is not an issue for a simple linear regression or when the predictors are orthogonal. But you should be careful with the interpretation of the BMA results as partial regression coefficients if the orthogonality does not hold. See Interpretation of BMA regression coefficients in BMA bmaregress.

sections.And what does low, negative, or missing: In bmaregress, sampling correlation is used to evaluate the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) convergence of the Bayesian model averaging (BMA) model. Sampling correlation is defined as the correlation between the analytical posterior model probabilities (PMPs) and their MCMC estimates based on sampling frequencies. It measures the agreement between the expected and observed PMPs. When sampling correlation is negative or has a low positive value (less than 10%), the nonconvergence is suspected. You should review your model specification carefully and potentially increase the MCMC sampling size by specifying the mcmcsize() option. Sampling correlation can also be missing. This is always the case when there is only one visited model. It is possible that there is only one plausible model in the BMA model space, which BMA found. In this case, there is no reason to suspect nonconvergence. However, in general, unless the regression model has no covariates, one visited model is insufficient to explore the full model domain, and you should not trust the reported results. This may happen when there is an insufficient number of MCMC iterations. These can be increased by specifying mcmcsize(). Sampling correlation is not a formal measure of MCMC convergence. Its precision may vary from one sample to another. In fact, when the g parameter of the Zellner's g-prior used for the regression coefficients is random, there is no reliable way to estimate sampling correlation. This is because there is no analytical formula for PMPs. In this case, sampling correlation is computed based on the harmonic-mean approximation of the analytical PMP distribution and is thus subject to the accuracy of the approximation, in addition to the inherent sampling variability. You should interpret a sampling-correlation value as a guide for the MCMC convergence rather than using it as a formal assessment of the convergence. There is no formal way to determine MCMC convergence. Sampling correlation is just one way to explore MCMC convergence numerically. You should also look at graphical convergence diagnostics (see bmagraph pmp and Convergence of BMA in BMA bmaregress) and other standard MCMC diagnostics tools (see, for example, Convergence of MCMC in BAYES bayesmh).

name: j_bmastats_msize_mps
title: Analytical and frequency model-size distributions and their summaries

sections.Analytical and frequency model-size dist: bmastats msize reports prior and posterior model-size summaries. bmagraph msize plots prior and posterior model-size distributions. They use labels Analytical and Frequency in the output. Analytical refers to a model-size distribution and its summaries that use model probabilities computed using analytical formulas. Frequency refers to those that use frequency estimates of model probabilities based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sample. Not all computations are available in all cases. In what follows, when we say "model-size summaries", we imply the model-size distribution as well. Analytical prior model-size summaries are always available, with a caveat that in cases when the model space is not explored fully, these analytical summaries are conditional on the visited models. Analytical posterior model-size summaries are available only when g is fixed in Zellner's g-prior, which is used for regression coefficients. Frequency posterior model-size summaries are available only when an MCMC sample of models is available, such as in the case of random g. The MCMC sample is also available for fixed g if you use the MCMC sampling, option sampling, with bmaregress.

name: j_bmastatsjoint_undefined
title: Some jointness measures undefined in bmastats jointness

sections.Some jointness measures undefined in bma: There are cases when jointness measures are not defined. bmastats jointness reports a missing value in those cases for the corresponding pair of variables. Below, we list, separately for each type of jointness measure, the conditions under which the measures are defined. Jointness measures are defined for a pair of two different variables, x1 and x2. Doppelhofer and Weeks jointness measure is defined when there is at least one model in each of the following four cases: 1. Both x1 and x2 are included. 2. Both x1 and x2 are excluded. 3. x1 is included but x2 is excluded. 4. x1 is excluded but x2 is included. Ley and Steel (type 1) jointness measure is defined if not all models that include x1 also include x2 and vice versa. Ley and Steel (type 2) jointness measure is defined if there is a model that includes x1 but not x2 or vice versa. Yule's Q measure of jointness is defined if at least one of the following two conditions is satisfied: 1. There is a model that includes both x1 and x2, and there is a model that excludes both x1 and x2. 2. There is a model that includes x1 and excludes x2, and there is a model that includes x2 and excludes x1. Modified Yule's Q measure of jointness is always defined when it is available. This measure is available with sampling methods when you also specify the frequency option to perform computations based on Markov chain Monte Carlo frequency-based estimates of posterior model probabilities.

name: j_cfactor
title: Specifying factor variables for crossed-effects models

sections.Specifying factor variables for crossed-: The crossed-effects factor-variable specification, R.varname, is typically used for fitting crossed-effects models. Indicator variables are included for all levels of the crossed-effects factor variable, and the constant is omitted. The variances of the random coefficients for these indicators are constrained to be equal.

sections.What is chibar2?: The likelihood-ratio (LR) test that is displayed is testing on the boundary of the parameter space. You are probably testing whether an estimated variance component (something that is always greater than 0) is different from 0 by using an LR test. Suppose for now that the two models being compared differ only with respect to the variance component in question, in which case the test statistic will be displayed as "chibar(01)". In such cases, the limiting distribution of the maximum likelihood estimate of the parameter in question is a normal distribution that is halved or chopped off at the boundary (here 0). The distribution of the LR test statistic is therefore not the usual chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom but is instead a 50:50 mixture of a chi-squared with no degrees of freedom (that is, a point mass at zero) and a chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom. The p-value of the LR test takes this into account and will be set to 1 if it is determined that your estimate is close enough to 0 to be, in effect, 0 for purposes of significance. Otherwise, the p-value displayed is set to one-half of the probability that a chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom is greater than the calculated LR test statistic. Sometimes you are testing whether a variance component is zero in addition to testing whether k other parameters (not affected by boundary conditions) are zero. Such situations often arise when comparing mixed-effects models. For such tests, the distribution of the likelihood-ratio test statistic is a 50:50 mixture of chi-squared distributions with k and k+1 degrees of freedom, shown on the output as "chibar(4_5)", for example. As for chibar(01), significance levels are adjusted accordingly. Finally, if you are testing more than one boundary-affected parameter, the theory is much more complex and usually intractable. When this occurs, Stata either will display significance levels that are conservative and marked as such or will not display an LR test at all.

sections.Conservative confidence intervals: Confidence interval is wider than requested. The computation of the confidence interval uses a bisection optimization algorithm. If there are t-statistics that have exactly the same value across bootstrap replications, the algorithm will not solve exactly for the requested confidence level.

name: j_cluster_multiway_pd
title: Multiway-cluster variance-covariance matrix is not positive semidefinite

sections.Multiway-cluster variance-covariance mat: You requested a multiway-cluster variance-covariance matrix of the estimators (VCE) by specifying option vce(cluster clustvar). This matrix is not positive semidefinite. Negative eigenvalues have been replaced with 0s to make the VCE positive semidefinite. Inference may be unreliable; see Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2011) for details.
sections.Reference: Cameron, A. C., J. B. Gelbach, and D. L. Miller. 2011. Robust inference with multiway clustering. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 29: 238-249. //doi.org/10.1198/jbes.2010.07136".

name: j_cmrisk
title: Odds ratios and relative-risk ratios in multinomial choice models

sections.Odds ratios and relative-risk ratios in: Choice models fit by cmclogit, cmmixlogit, and cmxtmixlogit display exponentiated coefficients when the or option is specified. These models allow both alternative-specific and case-specific covariates, and the interpretation of exponentiated coefficients differs depending on the type of covariate. For alternative-specific variables, the exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios, as the option name implies. However, for case-specific variables, exponentiated coefficients are interpreted as relative-risk ratios, similar to a conventional multinomial logistic regression as fit by mlogit with the rrr option.

sections.Adding tags to collected results: Values in a collection are organized according to tags. These tags are later used to lay out and customize a table. Stata automatically adds tags to each value in the collection when the results are collected. You may add your own tags as well. A tag comprises dimensions and levels and is written as dimension[level]. For example, if you are collecting results from a regression model and want to tag these results with the dimension model and the level 1, you can type model[1] The level may also be a string, so you can instead type model[reduced] If the string includes spaces, it must be enclosed in quotation marks such as model["M 1"] You may attach more than one tag to your collected results. You could type, for instance, model[1] group[A] See TABLES Intro 2 to learn more about tags, dimensions, and levels.

name: j_dsgenl_steady
title: Why are some standard errors reported missing?

sections.Why are some standard errors reported mi: Standard errors are not computed for some values reported in estat steady, estat policy, and estat transition after dsgenl. This is because of the structure of the equations in your model. The structure can lead to situations in which the steady-state values of variables, their policy parameters, or their transition parameters do not depend on any of the parameters estimated in the model. They are therefore constrained to the values reported by the estat commands. No standard errors are estimated for these constrained values. Note that steady-state, policy, and transition values may have implied constraints even when there are no constraints specified in dsgenl.

name: j_fp_testdf
title: Degrees of freedom for comparing fractional polynomial models

sections.Degrees of freedom for comparing fractio: When fp is used to search for the best combination of powers, it reports a table comparing fractional polynomial models of different degrees. In this table, the Test df column does not correspond to the model degrees of freedom for the individual models but rather to the degrees of freedom of a test comparing that model with the model with the lowest deviance. For normal error models, this is the numerator degrees of freedom of a partial F test; for other models, it is the degrees of freedom of the likelihood-ratio chi-squared test. In either case, the test degrees of freedom accounts for the two types of parameters that are being estimated by fp: coefficients and powers. Because the powers in a fractional polynomial are chosen from a finite set rather than from the entire real line, the degrees of freedom defined in this way are approximate and generally yield somewhat conservative tests (Royston and Altman 1994). See Methods and formulas in [R] fp for further details.
sections.Reference: Royston, P., and D. G. Altman. 1994. Regression using fractional polynomials of continuous covariates: Parsimonious parametric modelling. Applied Statistics 43: 429–467.

name: j_glmadmiss
title: My glm output reports that some mean estimates are inadmissible

sections.My glm output reports that some mean est: Your estimation results show that your parameter estimates produce inadmissible mean predictions for one or more observations in your estimation sample. As a result, you should exercise caution in interpreting these parameter estimates. If you obtained this warning, then you have attempted to fit a binomial model with either log or identity link. If you fit a binomial model with log link either via glm or binreg with option rr for risk ratios, then the warning arose because the linear predictor (eta in glm jargon) is greater than zero for one or more observations. For this model, the estimated probability of a positive event is the exponentiated linear predictor. When the linear predictor is greater than zero, the estimated probability is greater than one, which is inadmissible. If you fit a binomial model with identity link either via glm or binreg with option rd for risk differences, then the warning arose because the linear predictor is outside the range [0,1] for one or more observations. As such, the predicted probability of a positive event (which is just the linear predictor in this case) is outside its admissible range for these observations. Most likely your model was fit via ML and the estimation algorithm did not converge. Even if the algorithm did converge, the interpretation of the resulting parameter estimates is questionable.

name: j_gsd_infofrac
title: Spacing of looks in a group sequential design

sections.Spacing of looks in a group sequential d: By default, gsdesign rounds sample sizes up to whole numbers, which can cause the information fraction attained to differ from the information fraction requested. For fractional sample sizes that produce the requested information fraction, specify option nfractional. See example 1 in Remarks and examples of [ADAPT] gsdesign for a demonstration.

name: j_gsd_pvalues
title: Assumption of normality in a group sequential design

sections.Assumption of normality in a group seque: A group sequential design assumes that a hypothesis test is conducted at each look, and the test statistics follow a multivariate normal distribution with a specific covariance structure; see Methods and formulas in [ADAPT] gsbounds. This assumption is automatically satisfied for hypothesis tests that rely on the normality assumption, such as a z test comparing one or two means with a known variance. Other hypothesis tests, such as the log-rank test of survivor functions and the large-sample test of the equality of proportions, are asymptotically normal. The boundary critical values for a group sequential design are reported on the z scale and are intended for direct comparison with test statistics that follow a standard normal distribution under the null hypothesis. Careful consideration is needed when this assumption might be violated, such as in the case of a t test comparing one or two means when the variance is unknown and the sample size is not large. In this case, you may not compare the boundary critical values directly with the t statistic from a t test. An alternative is to compare the p-value from the test with the p-value corresponding to the boundary critical value. This procedure is known as the significance level approach and is quite accurate as long as the assumption about the covariance structure of the test statistics is satisfied. Both gsbounds and gsdesign report p-value equivalents in the table of boundary critical values; however, they can be suppressed with the nopvalues option. See examples 2 and 3 in Remarks and examples of [ADAPT] gsdesign onemean; example 2 in Remarks and examples of [ADAPT] gsdesign twomeans; and examples 2 and 3 in Remarks and examples of [ADAPT] gsdesign twoproportions for a demonstration of the significance level approach. For formulas, see significance level approach in Methods and formulas of [ADAPT] gsbounds. Many popular statistical tests satisfy the assumption about the covariance structure, which is also known as the assumption of independent increments. Jennison and Turnbull (1999, 233) provide several examples of scenarios where this assumption does not hold, even asymptotically, such as the group sequential analysis of longitudinal data comparing the mean response of two groups, where the within-subject response has an autoregressive element. You should understand that the significance level approach does not justify the use of group sequential testing when the assumption of independent increments is violated; it applies only when this assumption is satisfied but the test statistics are not normally distributed.
sections.Reference: Jennison, C., and B. W. Turnbull. 1999. Group Sequential Methods with Applications to Clinical Trials. Boca Raton, FL: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

sections.Heterogeneous treatment timing: Treatment effects might differ for groups treated at different points in time. When you use didregress, you assume the treatment effect is the same regardless of the time of treatment. If you believe the treatment effect is not homogeneous because of the different treatment timings, consider using hdidregress instead of didregress.

sections.Simultaneous confidence intervals: Let ATET(g,t) denote the average treatment effects on the treated for cohort g at time t. Let b1 denote an aggregation of ATET(g,t) across cohorts and time. Suppose there are k requested aggregations, ranging from b1, b2, to bk. Then the simultaneous confidence intervals are guaranteed to cover all the requested aggregations with a probability of at least 1 - α. The simultaneous confidence intervals are computed using the multiplier bootstrap algorithm in Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021). Its construction uses the estimated standard errors from the bootstrapped samples.
sections.References: Callaway, B. and P. H. C. Sant'Anna. 2021. Difference-in-differences with multiple time periods. Journal of Econometrics 225: 200-230.

sections.Estimability of ATET parameters: Average treatment effect on the treated (ATET) parameter estimates in hdidregress twfe or xthdidregress twfe are shown as 0 (omitted) in output when these parameters cannot be uniquely determined from the available data. There are several reasons that an ATET parameter for a given cohort, time period, or combination of cohort and time period may not be estimable: 1. There are no observations for the combination of cohort and time period. (Note that if there are no observations for an entire cohort or a time period, then that cohort or time period will be dropped altogether, rather than its parameters marked as omitted.) Estimation of an ATET parameter for a combination of cohort and time period relies on observations from that cohort and time period. 2. There are no treated observations for the time period or combination of cohort and time period or no untreated observations for the time period. Estimation of an ATET parameter relies on the presence of relevant treated and untreated observations that can be compared. 3. There are no observations, no treated observations, or no untreated observations for some level of a factor covariate for the cohort, time period, or combination of cohort and time period. When covariates are included, the two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) method estimates regression coefficients for the interactions of the ATET parameters and the covariates. Estimation of the ATET parameters relies on estimability of the parameters associated with these interactions. 4. The variables used to compute the specified ATET are perfectly collinear with other variables in the regression and thus do not admit unique estimates. This often occurs if there are only a few observations of the associated cohort, time period, or cohort-time period when interacted with covariates. Reasons 1 and 2 are problems that can arise in models with or without covariates. Reason 3 is a problem that is particular to the choice of covariates for a given model, and this is generally true of reason 4 as well. Omitted ATET parameters in these cases can often be estimated if the covariate specification is made "coarser" (meaning there are fewer interaction terms for which we need to produce regression parameter estimates). As an example of an estimability problem that is specific to the covariate specification, the following hdidregress model produces an ATET that cannot be estimated in one of the cohort-years: . hdidregress twfe (y x i.b) (policy), group(state) time(year) If we remove the factor variable i.b from the list of covariates, which has the effect of making the covariate specification "coarser", then all ATET parameters can be estimated. . hdidregress twfe (y x) (policy), group(state) time(year) For all types of estimability problems, models with cohort-time ATET parameters that are not estimable may have estimable cohort ATET or time period ATET parameters that can be obtained by using options hettype(cohort) and hettype(time), respectively.

sections.Simultaneous confidence intervals: Let ATET(g,t) denote the average treatment effects on the treated for cohort g at time t. Then the simultaneous confidence intervals are guaranteed to cover ATET(g,t)'s across all the cohorts and periods with a probability of at least 1 - α. The simultaneous confidence intervals are computed using the multiplier bootstrap algorithm in Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021). Its construction uses the estimated standard errors from the bootstrapped samples.
sections.References: Callaway, B. and P. H. C. Sant'Anna. 2021. Difference-in-differences with multiple time periods. Journal of Econometrics 225: 200-230.

sections.Null hypotheses: 1. No effect: The endogenous variable does not affect the outcome variable. 2. Constant effect: The endogenous effects do not vary across estimated quantiles. 3. Dominance: The endogenous effects are greater than zero across estimated quantiles. 4. Exogeneity: The variable is exogenous instead of endogenous.

sections.Instrumental-variables SVAR model specif: An instrumental-variables structural vector autoregressive (VAR) model fits an underlying VAR and then estimates structural relationships between the VAR residuals and external instruments, also called proxies. The lags(), noconstant, and exog() options apply to the underlying VAR. To view the full VAR output, specify the showgmm option. The zlags() and nozconstant options apply to the instruments themselves. You may wish to remove lags or a constant from the instrument. These options allow you to do so.

sections.Requirements for inference: The ds, po, and xpo commands, like other estimation procedures, require certain conditions be met so that their inferential results are valid. In addition, the plugin and CV selection methods have distinct properties and may perform differently under some conditions.
sections.Remarks: We assume you have read LASSO Lasso inference intro. We fit a model with, for example, dsregress with the default plugin selection method, and then we refit the model using CV. We get slightly different results. Which is correct? Plugin and CV are more than just different numerical techniques for model estimation. They make different assumptions, have different requirements, and have different properties. Asking which is correct has only one answer. Each is correct when their assumptions and requirements are met. In terms of practical advice, we have two alternative recommendations. The first one involves lots of computer time. 1. Fit the model with xpo and the default plugin. 2. Fit the model with xpo and CV. 3. Compare results. If they are similar, use the results from step 1. This alternative will save computer time. 1. Fit the model with ds with the default plugin. 2. Fit it again with ds but with CV. 3. Fit it again with po with the default plugin. 4. Fit it again with po but with CV. 5. Compare results. If they are similar, you are likely on solid ground. If so, perform step 6. 6. Fit the model again with xpo with the default plugin and use those results. You can combine these two recommendations. Start with the alternative, and if it fails at step 5, follow the first set of recommendations.

sections.Lasso with clustered data: Specifying a cluster variable will affect how the log-likelihood function is computed and how the sample is split in cross-validation. The log-likelihood function is computed as the sum of the log likelihood at the cluster levels. If option selection(cv) is specified, the cross-validation sample is split by the clusters defined by clustvar. That is, the subsample in each fold is drawn on the cluster level. Therefore, all observations in a cluster are kept together in the same subsample.

sections.What is the Laplacian approximation?: The Laplacian approximation is a computationally efficient method of calculating the log likelihood in a generalized linear mixed-effects model.
sections.How is the Laplacian approximation calcu: Calculating the log likelihood in a mixed-effects model requires integrating out the random effects, which are assumed to be normally distributed, so that the likelihood may be expressed as a function of the fixed effects and the variance components that summarize the random effects. When the response is non-Gaussian (binary, for instance), the integral has no closed form and must instead be approximated by some other means. The Laplacian method handles this task by approximating the integrand with a normal distribution centered at the values of the random effects that maximize the integrand. These maximizers correspond to the modes of the posterior distributions of the random effects given the response. Another way to estimate the integral is by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and this method is also available in generalized linear mixed-effects commands. Adaptive quadrature is merely plain quadrature in which the quadrature abscissas are adjusted to better capture the features of the integrand. In meglm and other generalized linear mixed-effects commands, the Laplacian approximation is equivalent to the mode-curvature adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with one integration point as described in Skrondal and Rabe-Hesketh (2004). The Laplacian approximation is quadrature performed using one abscissa, the mode itself. Because the Laplacian approximation involves only one abscissa, estimation can be much faster than adaptive quadrature using many abscissas. Of course, there is a price to be paid for this speed. Parameter estimates based on the Laplacian approximation tend to exhibit more bias than those based on multiabscissa adaptive quadrature, with the bias diminishing as the number of abscissas (and the computation time involved) increases.
sections.If Laplacian estimates are biased, why s: Despite its simplicity, the Laplacian approximation can perform well (Liu and Pierce 1994; Tierney and Kadane 1986), and on the basis of our own empirical evidence and the simulation studies of Pinheiro and Chao (2006), bias tends to be more prominent in the estimated variance components than in the estimated fixed effects. If you are more interested in inference on fixed effects adjusted for multilevel random effects than in estimates of the variance components that summarize the random effects, then the Laplacian approximation may be adequate for your needs. Also, the Laplacian approximation often produces a good approximation of the overall model log likelihood. Therefore, the Laplacian approximation can be useful during the model-building phase of your analysis as you compare competing models with LR tests (which are based on log likelihoods) before settling on a final model.
sections.References: Liu, Q., and D. A. Pierce. 1994. A note on Gauss-Hermite quadrature. Biometrika 81: 624-629. Pinheiro, J. C., and E. C. Chao. 2006. Efficient Laplacian and adaptive Gaussian quadrature algorithms for multilevel generalized linear mixed models. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 15: 58-81. Skrondal, A., and S. Rabe-Hesketh. 2004. //www.stata.com/bookstore/generalized-latent-variable-modeling/":Generalized Latent Variable Modeling: Multilevel, Longitudinal, and Structural Equation Models. Boca Raton, FL: Chapman & Hall/CRC. Tierney, L., and J. B. Kadane. 1986. Accurate approximations for posterior moments and marginal densities. Journal of the American Statistical Association 81: 82-86.

sections.What is linearization log likelihood?: menl uses the term linearization log likelihood to refer to the value of the objective function used in the optimization. menl uses the linearization method of Lindstrom and Bates (1990), with extensions from Pinheiro and Bates (1995), for estimation. The linearization method uses a first-order Taylor-series expansion of the specified nonlinear mean function to approximate it with a linear function of fixed and random effects. As a result, a nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) model is approximated by a linear mixed-effects (LME) model, in which the fixed-effects and random-effects design matrices involve derivatives of the nonlinear mean function with respect to fixed effects (coefficients) and random effects, respectively. Linearization log likelihood is the value of the log likelihood of this approximating LME model.
sections.References: Lindstrom, M. J., and D. M. Bates. 1990. Nonlinear mixed effects models for repeated measures data. Biometrics 46: 673-687. Pinheiro, J. C., and D. M. Bates. 1995. Approximations to the log-likelihood function in the nonlinear mixed-effects model. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 4: 12-35.

sections.Try nonlinear warning message: A marginal effect is a derivative. To find a derivative numerically, mfx uses the approximation (f(x+h)-f(x))/h. Thus, mfx must find a suitable change h that is small enough for the approximation to be accurate but not so small that the division of two small numbers would be inaccurate. mfx finds this change h by selecting an initial h and then looping, making h smaller or larger each time through the loop until it finds a suitable h. This process can be very time consuming for models with many variables, so you may want to avoid this by using another method, which we call the "linear method". This method uses a different set of formulas so that only a few derivatives have to be found. All the remaining derivatives can be obtained without iteration. If mfx has trouble obtaining the h for the few derivatives it must calculate using iteration, you can always use the usual "nonlinear" method. This will be slower, but because it is a different calculation, it may not have the same problem.

sections.Rescaling warning message: A marginal effect is a derivative. To find a derivative numerically, mfx uses the approximation (f(x+h)-f(x))/h. Thus mfx must find a suitable change h that is small enough for the approximation to be accurate but not so small that the division of two small numbers would be inaccurate. Usually mfx has no trouble doing this in obtaining a marginal effect, which is the derivative of the prediction function with respect to each independent variable x. To calculate the standard error of a marginal effect, mfx uses the delta method and must calculate the derivative of the marginal effect with respect to each coefficient in the model. To do this, mfx looks for a suitable small change in the coefficient b. Problems arise when a small change in b causes a large change in marginal effect, making it difficult for mfx to find a suitable change in b. The warning message is issued after mfx has gone though 50 iterations of its search for a suitable change. The message shows which variable had the problem. Rescaling that variable means dividing or multiplying the variable by a number and then running the estimation command again before running mfx again. When you divide a variable by, say, 100, both the marginal effect of that variable and its standard error are divided by 100, meaning that we get the same test statistic and p-value. The marginal effects and standard errors of other variables will be unchanged; however mfx may be more successful in its search for a suitable change in b.

sections.Predict expression unsuitable error mess: A marginal effect is a derivative of a function of the coefficients and independent variables of a model. The mfx option predict() can be used to specify the function to be differentiated. If this function depends on quantities other than the coefficients and independent variables of the model, mfx will most likely not be able to evaluate the derivative accurately. mfx checks for dependence on other quantities by predicting into different observations in the dataset and checking that it obtains the same value. If not, it determines that the expression is unsuitable. The mfx option diagnostics(beta) displays the results of these checks. The option force can be used to force the calculation of the marginal effect, although this is usually inadvisable.

sections.My {cmd:mi impute mvn: output indicates that EM did not converge
sections.EM is used to obtain starting values: Multivariate-normal imputations are obtained from an iterative Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method as draws from the posterior predictive distribution of the missing data given the observed data. The starting point of this chain is determined by EM parameter estimates of this predictive distribution. When EM does not converge, this indicates that 1) the starting point for the MCMC was less than optimal and 2) it is possible that the imputation model is not well suited to the data. The first item is not a serious problem provided that the MCMC burn-in period was sufficient to counteract a bad starting point. The second item is more serious and requires model adjustment.
sections.What do I do about this?: First, try increasing the number of EM iterations, thus giving EM a better chance of converging; see the iterate() option under em_options in mi impute mvn for how to change the maximum number of EM iterations. If increasing the number of iterations does not result in EM convergence, then examine the convergence properties of MCMC to ensure that there is no bigger issue. See example 4 (and following) of MI mi impute mvn for how to do this. If the diagnostics indicate a nonstable MCMC, increasing the burn-in and burn-between periods (the burnin() and burnbetween() options, respectively) may help. If the diagnostics do not indicate a nonstable MCMC, you may need to consider an alternate imputation model, such as one with a different set of predictors.

name: j_mixed_ddf
title: Why is small-sample inference not available or denominator degrees of freedom missing?

sections.Why is small-sample inference not availa: When you fit a mixed model and specify option dfmethod(), perform linear hypotheses tests using test, small or testparm, small after mixed, dfmethod(), or perform tests of contrasts using contrast, small after mixed, dfmethod(), you may see a missing value for the denominator degrees of freedom (DDF) of the reported F test. You may also see a note that small-sample inference is not available when you use lincom, small, contrast, small, or pwcompare, small after mixed, dfmethod(). This may occur when you use dfmethod(anova) or dfmethod(repeated). dfmethod(anova) and dfmethod(repeated) cannot compute DDF for a multiple-hypotheses F test when the degrees of freedom of the corresponding single-hypothesis t tests are not the same. Also, dfmethod(anova) and dfmethod(repeated) cannot compute DDF for a linear combination of fixed effects that have different DDFs. In these cases, small-sample inference is not available.

name: j_mixedlr
title: Why is my mixed-effects model LR test conservative?

sections.Why is my mixed-effects model LR test co: You have performed a likelihood-ratio (LR) test comparing two nested mixed-effects models, whether it be 1) the test versus a marginal regression presented at the bottom of the output produced by a mixed-effects command, or 2) the comparison of two mixed-effects models via lrtest. What follows below discusses the first scenario but applies equally to the second.
sections.Distribution theory for mixed-model comp: The LR test presented at the bottom of a mixed-effects command output is a comparison of the fitted mixed model to standard regression with no group-level random effects. For example, for melogit you are comparing with standard logistic regression. This LR test assesses whether all random-effects parameters of the mixed model are simultaneously zero. When there is only one random-effects parameter to be tested, this parameter, a variance component, is restricted to be greater than zero. Because the null hypothesis is that this parameter is indeed zero, which is on the boundary of the parameter space, the distribution of the LR test statistic is a 50:50 mixture of a chi2(0) (point mass at zero) and a chi2(1) (point mass at one) distribution. Therefore, significance levels in the one-parameter case can be adjusted accordingly, and no warning that the test is conservative is displayed. See Self and Liang (1987) for the appropriate theory, or see Gutierrez, Carter, and Drukker (2001) for a Stata-specific discussion. When there is more than one random-effects parameter to be tested, however, the situation becomes more complicated. Consider a model where we have two random coefficients with the unstructured covariance matrix + + | v_11 v_12 | | v_12 v_22 | + + Because the "random" component of the mixed model comprises three parameters (v_11,v_12,v_22), it would appear that the LR comparison test would be distributed as chi2(3). However, there are two complications that need to be considered. First, the variances v_11 and v_22 are restricted to be positive, and testing them against zero presents the same boundary condition described above. Second, constraints such as v_11 = 0 implicitly restrict the covariance v_12 to be zero as well, and from a technical standpoint, it is unclear how many parameters need to be restricted to reduce the model to one with no group-level random effects. Because of these complications, appropriate and sufficiently general computation methods for the more-than-one-parameter case have yet to be developed. Theory (for example, Stram and Lee [1994]) and empirical studies (for example, McLachlan and Basford [1988]) have demonstrated that, whatever the distribution of the LR test statistic, its tail probabilities are bound above by those of the chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the full number of restricted parameters (three in the above example). Mixed-effects commands use this reference distribution, the chi-squared test with full degrees of freedom, to produce a conservative test.
sections.How do I interpret the results of this c: The reported significance level for the LR test is an upper bound on the actual significance level. Rejection of the null hypothesis on the basis of the reported level would therefore imply rejection based on the actual level.

name: j_multipredictwarn
title: Average predictions with multiple-record survival data

sections.Average predictions with multiple-record: When there are multiple records per individual in survival analysis, average predictions over the dataset (usually computed by margins) may not be appropriate. A valid alternative is to use the at() option to compute predictions at fixed values of the covariates. The command margins computes, by default, predictive margins, also called adjusted predictions. When there is only one record per subject, the average prediction over the sample is an estimate of such prediction for the population. However, when there are multiple observations per individual, different individuals may have different numbers of observations. If we average those values, some individuals will be represented one time, and some individuals will be represented many times. This average value will not have a useful interpretation with respect to the population. With multiple-record survival-time data, an alternative is to use margins with the at() option to compute predictions at specific covariate patterns of interest.

sections.Group and time combinations: The following group and time combinations imply a difference-in-differences model: o One group variable and one time variable o Two group variables Otherwise, you are specifying a difference-in-difference-in-differences model.

sections.Macro average OVR AUC and AUCPR: For multiclass classification, when the auc option is specified, h2oml gbmultclass and h2oml rfmultclass compute AUC and AUCPR using macro average one versus rest, which is a uniform weighted average of all AUC scores calculated for each class versus the rest of the classes. For definitions, see metric_option H2OML.

name: j_permute_approx
title: Approximate standard errors and confidence intervals for two-sided p-values

sections.Approximate standard errors and confiden: Standard errors and confidence intervals for one-sided p-values are calculated as follows. The p-value is the proportion of permutations having test statistics that are more extreme than the test statistic observed in the original data. Its standard error and confidence interval are based on the binomial distribution as described in Methods and formulas in [R] permute. The confidence interval is an exact confidence interval. For two-sided p-values, standard errors and confidence intervals are only approximate. permute calculates the two-sided p-value as p = 2*min(p_lower, p_upper), where p_lower is the lower one-sided p-value and p_upper the upper one-sided p-value. Because this definition does not yield a simple formula for the standard error or confidence interval, the following ad hoc procedure is used. If p_lower is the minimum one-sided p-value, its count c is doubled. If p_upper is the minimum one-sided p-value, its count c is doubled. The distribution of this doubled count c2 is assumed to be approximately binomial. Its standard errors and confidence intervals are computed using . cii proportions n c2, wald where n is the number of permutations. The confidence intervals are asymptotic confidence intervals.

name: j_permute_error
title: Monte Carlo errors in permutation tests

sections.Monte Carlo errors in permutation tests: Because permutation tests are performed via a Monte Carlo procedure, the calculated p-values are approximations to the true exact p-values. permute reports a standard error and confidence interval for each p-value. The standard errors and confidence intervals are not used for traditional inference but instead are used to determine whether more permutations are necessary to increase the precision of the p-values. To make standard errors smaller and confidence intervals narrower, use the reps(#) option to increase the number of permutations. For information on the estimation of standard errors and p-values, see Methods and formulas in [R] permute.

name: j_reri_err
title: Nonpositive estimates for excess relative risk

sections.Nonpositive estimates for excess relativ: When one or more interactions have a nonpositive estimate for excess relative risk, the relative excess risk due to interaction statistic, attributable proportion, and synergy index may be difficult to interpret. These statistics assume that each of the three interactions of interest (-+, +-, and ++) has a relative risk greater than 1, which implies ERR = RR - 1 is greater than 0. Nonpositive excess relative risk estimates may be due to incorrectly specified base levels for the variables representing the exposures of interest. Base levels should be chosen so that a positive exposure is hypothesized to be associated with a greater probability of a positive outcome. See example 4 in [R] reri.

name: j_robustsingular
title: The F or chi2 model statistic has been reported as missing

sections.The F or chi2 model statistic has been r: Your estimation results show an F or a chi-squared model statistic reported to be missing. Stata has done that so as to not be misleading, not because there is something necessarily wrong with your model.
sections.Are any standard errors missing?: If any standard errors are reported as dots, something is wrong with your model: one or more coefficients could not be estimated in the normal statistical sense. You need to address that problem and ignore the rest of this discussion.
sections.Are you using a {cmd:svy: estimator or did you specify the vce(cluster clustvar) option?
sections.Is there a regressor that is nonzero for: The VCE you have just estimated is not of sufficient rank to perform the model test. This can happen if there is a variable in your model that is nonzero for only 1 observation in the estimation sample. Likewise, it can happen if a variable is nonzero for only one cluster when using the cluster-robust VCE. In such cases the derivative of the sum-of-squares or likelihood function with respect to that variable's parameter is zero for all observations. That implies that the outer-product-of-gradients (OPG) variance matrix is singular. Because the OPG variance matrix is used in computing the robust variance matrix, the latter is therefore singular as well.

sections.if() versus if exp: Both the if exp qualifier and the if(exp) option select records for which exp is true. We strongly recommend specifying the if() option in preference to the if exp qualifier. They differ in that the if exp qualifier removes data from consideration before calculating beginning and ending times and other quantities as well. The if() option, on the other hand, sets the restriction after all derived variables are calculated. The only reason to specify the if exp qualifier is to ignore errors in the data—observations that would confuse stset and streset—without actually dropping the offending observations from the dataset. You specify the if() option to exclude observations that are not themselves errors. Specifying if() yields the same result as specifying if exp on the subsequent st commands after the dataset has been stset. For more details, see if() versus if exp in [ST] stset.

name: j_stintcox_statusmiss
title: Missing values in option status() of command stintcox

sections.Missing values in option status() of com: When you specify option statussysmissok with stintcox, system missing values (.) in the event-time variable statusvar specified in option status() have a special meaning. The observations with system missing statusvar are excluded from the calculations used to determine the event-time intervals and censoring types of the corresponding subjects. But these observations are still used during estimation to provide covariate values at the specified examination times. If you have observations that you need to exclude from all computations, use extended missing values for those observations. Option statussysmissok can be useful to create time-varying covariates in a multiple-record-per-subject format; see Single- versus multiple-record interval-censored data formats in [ST] stintcox.

name: j_stintcox_variablese
title: Standard error estimation with interval-censored data

sections.Standard error estimation with interval-: With interval-censored data, the nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimation approach estimates regression coefficients jointly with the contributions to the baseline cumulative hazard function, which is infinite-dimensional. Thus, the classical estimator based on the entire information matrix does not provide a valid estimator of the variance{ch_endash}covariance matrix (VCE). Instead, the VCE for regression coefficients is estimated based on the profile log likelihood, which is obtained by maximizing the likelihood over the baseline hazard contributions by holding the regression coefficients fixed. Different methods are available to estimate the VCE for regression coefficients. For small datasets or datasets with low proportions of interval-censored observations, they may produce, sometimes noticeably, different results. It is important to investigate such cases more carefully and perhaps adjust the default tolerance to obtain more precise results. See Standard error estimation with interval-censored data in stintcox ST.

sections.Structural function interpretation: For derivatives and contrasts to have an average structural function interpretation, they must be computed conditioning on the value of the residuals. For this to be true, all instrumental variables and endogenous variables must be set to their original values for the residual computation using the base() or target() option. For derivatives and contrasts to have a fixed average structural function interpretation, the correlations that give rise to endogeneity must be fixed to zero. You may do this using the fix() or target() option. If your specification satisfies either of the conditions above, the results from margins have a structural function interpretation. Otherwise, they do not. You may use the default asf prediction to get an average structural function interpretation or fixedasf for a fixed average structural function interpretation. For a more detailed discussion about structural functions and their interpretation, see Remarks and examples in [ERM] Intro 7.

name: j_stslist_netlost
title: What is net lost, and why is it sometimes negative?

sections.What is net lost, and why is it sometime: Net lost is defined as the number lost or censored minus the number who entered. sts list reports net lost instead of the number lost (in the fourth column) with complicated survival data -- data with delayed entry or gaps or, more generally, with multiple records per subject. The notion of "lost" can mean many things with complicated survival data. A subject may be truly lost at time t, or the subject may leave at time t only to reenter at time t+1 with a different value of covariates. And there are other possibilities. In such cases, net lost represents the number really lost if there are no gaps or delayed entry. For instance, if there are three subjects lost at time t but three more enter, no one is lost time t, and net lost properly reflects this. Consequently, if more subjects enter at time t than are lost, net lost will be negative, meaning a gain in the number of subjects. You can specify the enter option to report both the pure number lost and the number who entered instead of a single net lost, but the pure number lost should be interpreted in combination with the number who entered. In our example, the pure number lost is three, but because three subjects enter, the actual number lost is zero. See Counting the number lost to censoring in [ST] sts.

name: j_vuong
title: Vuong test is not appropriate for testing zero inflation

sections.Vuong test is not appropriate for testin: Greene (1994) proposed using the Vuong test for nonnested models (Vuong 1989) to test for zero inflation. Despite many earlier citations, recent work by Wilson (2015) has shown that the Vuong test is inappropriate for testing zero inflation. Nesting occurs when the probability of zero inflation is 0, which is on the boundary, and this violates the regularity conditions of the Vuong test for nonnested models. So the distribution of the test statistic is not standard normal. The actual distribution is unknown and thus cannot be used for inference. You may consider using information criteria to choose between the standard and the zero-inflated models; see example 2 in [R] zip.
sections.References: Greene, W. H. 1994. Accounting for excess zeros and sample selection in Poisson and negative binomial regression models. Working paper EC-94-10, Department of Economics, Stern School of Business, New York University. //ideas.repec.org/p/ste/nystbu/94-10.html". Vuong, Q. H. 1989. Likelihood ratio tests for model selection and non-nested hypotheses. Econometrica 57: 307-333. Wilson, P. 2015. The misuse of the Vuong test for non-nested models to test for zero-inflation. Economics Letters 127: 51-53.
